analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicaid insulin prices to all diagnosed diabetics and caps insulin copays at $10 a month.
analysis.headline: The bill received no hearing, markup, or vote and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an "American Insulin Program" requiring insulin manufacturers to sell to anyone diagnosed with diabetes at the discounted prices they already charge Medicaid. It also capped insulin copays at $10 a month in Medicare and private insurance plans, banned the hidden rebate payments drugmakers make to pharmacy benefit managers for insulin, and directed a study of whether the federal government should manufacture insulin itself. The bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be people with diabetes who need insulin, especially the uninsured and people with high-deductible private plans, who would get the manufacturer's Medicaid price directly at the pharmacy. Medicare beneficiaries and people with employer or individual market plans would pay no more than $10 a month in insulin cost-sharing.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to sign agreements with insulin manufacturers so that any individual with a diagnosed diabetes can access Medicaid-level prices for insulin at the pharmacy point of sale, whether or not they are on Medicaid.
Caps insulin cost-sharing at $10 per month in private group and individual health plans and in Medicare Part D, beginning 90 days after enactment.

Eliminates the federal anti-kickback safe harbor that currently protects manufacturer rebates, discounts, and price concessions paid to pharmacy benefit managers for insulin, targeting the middleman payments that push list prices up.

Bars Medicaid managed-care contracts and pharmacy benefit managers from spread pricing (keeping the difference between what the state pays and what pharmacies receive), requires full pass-through of pharmacy payments, and freezes Medicaid supplemental rebate deals at current levels.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to report within 180 days on whether the federal government could feasibly and affordably manufacture insulin directly.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would bear the largest cost, extending their lowest negotiated prices to a far broader group of buyers. Pharmacy benefit managers would lose rebate and spread-pricing revenue on insulin. Insurers would absorb the $10 copay cap, though the bill offsets some of that by excluding insulin payments from the medical loss ratio denominator.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insulin manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The discounted Medicaid price applies only to individuals who have received a diabetes diagnosis, not to the drug market as a whole, so list prices for everyone else would stay untouched.
HHS would have to publish a model agreement for manufacturers just 20 days after enactment, drafted in consultation with the manufacturers themselves, which leaves little time for careful design.

A manufacturer can terminate its agreement for any reason, and the Secretary may raise the Medicaid price by 5 percent, up to three times, if the Secretary certifies that manufacturer revenues are unsustainable, giving the industry exits if the discounts bite.

The $10 copay cap shifts costs onto insurers and employers unless manufacturer prices fall far enough, and the bill's exclusion of insulin spending from the medical loss ratio calculation reduces the rebate dollars insurers otherwise owe consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — Medicaid-level insulin prices for anyone diagnosed with diabetes and a $10 monthly copay cap — is a substantial, direct benefit to the roughly one in ten Americans with diabetes, financed mainly by the three companies that dominate the insulin market and by middlemen whose rebates keep list prices high. The bill is narrowly drafted and has real design flaws, including the diagnosis-only requirement, the rushed 20-day rulemaking, and manufacturer exit clauses, but its costs fall overwhelmingly on concentrated industry rather than on taxpayers or consumers. The decisive fact is not the bill's quality but its fate: it drew no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and to a health subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Crist introduced the Affordable Insulin for All Act on February 4, 2020, to lower insulin prices through Medicaid-price access and a $10 monthly copay cap.
The bill was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on it.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, insulin manufacturers kept their existing pricing and rebate arrangements, and pharmacy benefit managers kept their rebate and spread-pricing revenue on insulin. People with diabetes continued to face the same insulin prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers and pharmacy benefit managers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern ever formed.

industries.note: The bill would require insulin makers to extend their lowest Medicaid-negotiated prices to every person diagnosed with diabetes, a major revenue concession for the small group of companies that dominate insulin. Their current pricing depends on high list prices offset by secret rebates, which the bill dismantles for insulin.

The bill removes the federal safe harbor that lets manufacturers pay PBMs rebates on insulin, and bans spread pricing in Medicaid, eliminating two of the middleman revenue streams that keep insulin list prices high.

Insurers would have to cap insulin cost-sharing at $10 a month, but the bill excludes insulin payments from the medical loss ratio denominator, making it easier for insurers to meet their rebate requirement. The net effect depends on how much manufacturer prices actually fall.

The Medicaid pass-through pricing requirement guarantees pharmacies are reimbursed ingredient cost plus a dispensing fee at least equal to what the state would pay directly, protecting them from spread-pricing squeeze.
